claims.text: A refractory eutectic high-entropy alloy can be engineered to exhibit a ductile-brittle-ductile transition as temperature increases.
The proposed alloy can be based on W together with refractory elements such as Nb, Mo, and Ta.
A hierarchical lamellar microstructure with coherent interfaces is responsible for the proposed temperature-dependent transition.
The coherent-interface microstructure avoids the usual temper embrittlement observed in conventional alloys.
The initial alloy is produced by rapid melting and solidification or a similar method.
The initial alloy has a two-phase lamellar structure.
The initial alloy is strong and ductile at room temperature.
Controlled heating and holding across a wide temperature range will be used to probe the mechanical response.
Tensile testing will be conducted under inert atmosphere at low, intermediate, and high temperatures.
Hierarchical coherent interphase boundaries help relieve or distribute interfacial stress.
The hierarchical coherent-interface microstructure promotes multiple deformation mechanisms.
At low temperatures, dislocation activity within coherent lamellae produces ductility.
At intermediate temperatures, localized stress concentration at phase boundaries causes brittle behavior.
At high temperatures, diffusion-enhanced recovery and greater dislocation mobility restore ductility.
High-temperature activation of stacking faults and deformation twins contributes to restored ductility.
The alloy will be ductile at ambient temperature, brittle over a narrow intermediate-temperature window, and ductile again at higher temperature.
Conventional tungsten-based or single-principal-element alloys generally undergo continuous temper embrittlement without recovery of ductility at elevated temperatures.
The transition is limited to eutectic high-entropy alloys with precisely controlled multiphase microstructures and may not occur in single-phase materials or other alloy families.
The temperatures and magnitudes of ductility loss and recovery depend on alloy composition and processing history.
